_phase: WT.0 — the AFG.3 tradition that needs NO engine work. Highlife is 12-TET and 4/4: Western guitars, Western horns, diatonic I-IV-V. What makes it highlife is the two-finger palm-wine picking, the bell, the offbeat and the horn voicings — all expressible in the existing role/degree space. Zero Swift.
name: Highlife
blurb: West African highlife: interlocking palm-wine guitar figures over a bright diatonic vamp, offbeat bell and a melodic bass that answers the guitar.

chords._comment: Bright and diatonic on purpose. Highlife harmony is major-key I-IV-V territory, so triads with the occasional 7th rather than the rootless 9ths a soul pack wants. barsPerChord 1 keeps the vamp turning over, which is what the guitar figures ride.

groove._comment: Offbeat, staccato and interlocking — the palm-wine guitar sits between the beats rather than on them. Short durations so the figures stay separate instead of blurring into a pad.
groove.name: stabs

bass._comment: Melodic and answering, not a root pedal — highlife bass moves with the guitar. rootFifth with a mid register keeps it singing rather than sub-heavy.

melody._comment: Horn-section lead. Program 56 (trumpet) is the highlife signature over a guitar bed.

flavors.label: Palm Wine
flavors.blurb: The old acoustic guitar-band feel: two chords, two-finger picking, unhurried and a little behind the beat.

flavors.label: Dance Band
flavors.blurb: E.T. Mensah territory - swing-band sevenths, full I-IV-V turnaround, horns answering the guitar.

flavors.label: Burger Highlife
flavors.blurb: Eighties synth highlife: drum-machine tight, short keyboard stabs, two chords rocking back and forth.

flavors.label: Gospel Highlife
flavors.blurb: Church highlife - sustained organ, hymn-sized changes, richer chords under a congregation melody.

flavors.label: Guitar Band Vamp
flavors.blurb: The long one-chord stretch a guitar band drops into so the interlocking parts can take over.

arranger.llmStyleBrief: Highlife is bright and diatonic: major-key I-IV-V with a turnaround through vi or ii, one chord per bar so the vamp keeps turning over. Sevenths come from the dance-band horn tradition; ninths and altered chords do not belong. Minor tunes borrow bVII rather than a raised leading tone. Keep the harmony simple - the interlocking guitars carry the interest.
